Red Umbrellas: First Sex Worker Pride March Organized in Boston History
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content_excerpt: The marchers in front of Jacque’s, the oldest continuously operating gay bar in Boston (Andrew S) By: Andrew S BOSTON COMMON – On September 14, sex workers and allies gathered at Brewer Fountain under a canopy of red umbrellas for Boston’s historic first March for Sex Worker Pride. Led by organizers Rita Romero from Red Light Disco, Amanda Rodriguez from FemMenThem, and Jessica Van Meir from Boston Sex Workers and Allies Collective (BSWAC), the march both centered the public celebration of sex worker pride and the ongoing fight for decriminalization. Several sex workers, community organizers, and local politicians spoke to a crowd about the importance of the event before participants marched from the Common to Jacques’ Cabaret, the oldest continuously operating gay bar in the city. articles.title: Brazil’s Presidential Election Is Going Down to the Wire
articles.author: Olavo Passos de Souza
articles.content_excerpt: As the Brazilian presidential election on October 4 draws closer, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is in a very tight contest with Flávio Bolsonaro, the son and heir of the Bolsonaro political dynasty. Lula is leading most of the polls for the first round, but the race appears too close to call in the event of a runoff between them. This election does not merely pit two opposing candidates against each other. It is a struggle between Brazil’s democratic forces and the return to power of a reactionary bloc. Lula’s Challenge Lula is seeking a fourth term as president at the age of eighty-one. The Brazilian constitution allows for this: it does not impose any limits on how long one person can be in office, so long as they do not serve more than two consecutive terms. articles.title: Amazon Is Perfecting Total Surveillance of Its Workforce
articles.author: C. R. Calabria
articles.content_excerpt: Although Amazon is increasingly synonymous with worker surveillance , the logistics behemoth has never been a pioneer in that space. UPS was the first fleet to install GPS in their vehicles back in 1991. Netradyne, the company that makes the AI-powered product Driver.i installed in most vehicles in Amazon’s fleet, had already logged over a hundred million minutes of driving time before Amazon signed the firm on. But with each new iteration of its delivery-aid-cum-surveillance tech, Amazon has proven its knack for taking an existing product and deploying it in a dystopian direction. articles.title: Primetime Turns Chris Hansen Into a Horror Show
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content_excerpt: Primetime has an interesting look that’s the key to its worldview, which is that our society is so bad that no one can escape its infecting qualities. There’s a smeary effect around the edge of the lens in many shots, which are generally in shallow focus, making everything appear greasy and defiled and half-hidden. This is in addition to a lurid color scheme dominated by nasty shades of red, green, and blue that are often clashing with each other, so that characters’ faces emerge out of surroundings that seem disgustingly tainted. Robert Pattinson, playing Chris Hansen — the real-life former host of the hit NBC Dateline series To Catch a Predator that ran from 2004 to 2007 — appears in certain close-ups with his face suffused in an unwholesome tint of hellfire red. articles.title: Economic Democracy Is at the Heart of Socialism
articles.author: Mike Beggs
articles.content_excerpt: In 1872, British courts prosecuted more than seventeen thousand workers for a single offense: leaving their jobs. Under the Master and Servants Acts, wage laborers who quit before the end of an agreed term, or who merely refused to show up to work, could be sentenced to three months of hard labor. Employers who violated the same rule, by withholding wages or firing someone without notice, owed just a civil debt. Across the 1860s and early 1870s, as the labor market tightened and approached full employment, the number of prosecutions rose. Even before the eight-hour day became one of organized labor’s defining demands, one of the British trade union movement’s earliest sustained legislative campaigns was to end the criminal punishment of workers who left their jobs. articles.title: Britain Used Modern Advertising to Sell Its Empire
articles.author: Owen Hatherley
articles.content_excerpt: The American empire has never needed a propaganda ministry to justify itself to its subjects. For that, it has the world’s largest culture industry. From Hollywood to hip-hop, it has made millions around the world dream of being American, even those who hate its politics and economics. But American cultural imperialism comes into focus only when examined against its immediate precursor. For all the British Empire spread — constitutional monarchies, tea drinking, bleakly Protestant Christianity, and ruthless, amoral capitalism — it never made its victims aspire to be British in quite the same way as its American offshoot has. articles.title: Faith-Labor Organizing: Why Building Permanent Infrastructure is the Intervention This Moment Demands
articles.content_excerpt: Featured image by Jared Rodriguez. Our congregations and our unions each have a measure of power. None of it is enough. The change we seek requires building power together; prioritizing building that power together in parallel with the work we are already doing alone. Our faith communities and labor unions share geographies, serve many of the same families, and claim a common commitment to human dignity. We rarely build power together. When we collaborate, the collaboration tends to be transactional: labor shows up for a rally the church organized, a pastor blesses a picket line. The event ends. Everyone goes home. articles.title: Trump’s Greenland Deal Puts His Annexation Plans on Ice
articles.author: Huw Paige
articles.content_excerpt: Donald Trump recently concluded an agreement with the governments of Greenland and Denmark over the status of the Arctic island. Trump presented it as a big victory for his efforts, claiming that it granted the United States “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many US concerns.” The substance of the agreement told a different story. After doing lasting damage to the relationship between the United States and Europe, the Trump administration got more or less the same deal it could have obtained by asking politely. Trump’s repeatedly stated plan to acquire Greenland has been put on the back burner.
